components.note: 亻 (person) — 偶 originally described a wooden figure or idol shaped like a person, later extending to 'a pair' and 'by chance.'
禺 (yú) gives a sound distantly related to 偶's reading ǒu, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I occasionally drink coffee.
example.fact: 偶尔 (ǒu'ěr, 'occasionally') is one of the most common words built on 偶, describing something that happens only now and then.

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辑 originally referred to fitting a cart's parts together, extending to 'gather, compile, edit.'
咠 (qì) is distantly related in sound to jí, sharing the same historical initial series (j/q/x) though the two have drifted apart.

example.english: She is a magazine editor.
example.fact: 编辑 (biānjí) pairs 编 ('to compile') with 辑 ('to edit') to name both the job and the action of editing.

etymologyHint: A bountiful 丰 place 阝

components.note: 丰 depicts a plant heavy with grain, a picture of abundance and plenty.
阝 (a settlement or region) — together with 丰, the image of an abundant place gave 邦 its meaning 'nation, state.'

example.pinyin: Zhōngguó shì yí gè dà bāng.
example.english: China is a great nation.
example.fact: 邦 mostly appears today inside compound words like 联邦 (liánbāng, 'federal') and 邻邦 (línbāng, 'neighboring country') rather than standing alone.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 恢 describes a broad, expansive mental capacity, as in 'to restore, magnanimous.'
灰 (huī) gives the sound — an exact match with 恢.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng bāng tā huīfù le jiànkāng.
example.english: The doctor helped him restore his health.
example.fact: 恢复 (huīfù, 'to restore, to recover') is the most common word built on 恢, often used for health or normal conditions returning.

components.note: 贝 (money, from ancient shell currency) — 赖 relates to depending on someone for support, as in 'to rely on.'
剌 (là) gives a sound close to lài, sharing the initial l- and a similar rhyme.

example.english: Small children rely heavily on their mothers.
example.fact: 依赖 (yīlài, 'to depend on') is a common word built on 赖, describing needing someone or something for support.

components.note: 囗 (enclosure) — 圈 describes an enclosed loop or pen, as in 'circle, corral.'
卷 (juǎn) shares the rhyme -uan with quān, though the initial has drifted from j- to q- over time.

example.english: The sheep are sleeping in the pen.
example.fact: 圈 names both a drawn circle and a fenced enclosure for animals, two closely related senses of 'a bounded loop.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摸 describes touching or feeling something with the hand.
莫 (mò) gives a sound very close to mō, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.pinyin: Tā mōle mō māo de tóu.
example.english: He gently touched the cat's head.
example.fact: 摸 is the everyday verb for touching or feeling something gently, often repeated as 摸一摸 or 摸了摸.

etymologyHint: To exalt 卬 a person 亻

components.note: 卬 depicts a person looking upward — 仰 keeps that upward gaze.
亻 (person) — a person 亻 looking upward 卬 gave 仰 its meaning 'to look up to, to admire.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn yǎngmù zhè wèi kēxuéjiā.
example.english: I greatly admire this scientist.
example.fact: 仰 almost always appears in 仰慕 (yǎngmù, 'to admire') and 信仰 (xìnyǎng, 'belief, faith').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 润 describes something made moist or glossy by water.
闰 (rùn) gives the sound — an exact match with 润.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yóu néng rùnhuá jīqì.
example.english: This oil can lubricate machines.
example.fact: 润 combines with 滑 to form 润滑 (rùnhuá, 'to lubricate'), a common technical word for reducing friction.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 堆 describes a mound or pile, often of earth or soil.
隹 (zhuī) shares the rhyme -uī with duī, though the initial has drifted from zh- to d- over time.

example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ yǒu yì duī shāzi.
example.english: There is a pile of sand in the yard.
example.fact: 堆 works as both a verb ('to pile up') and a measure word for heaps of loose material, like sand or snow.

components.note: 石 (rock) — 碰 originally described one hard object, like a stone, striking another, giving 'to bump, to collide.'
並 (bìng) is only distantly related in sound to pèng — both use a bilabial initial (b/p), but the rhyme and tone have drifted apart.

example.english: Be careful, don't bump into the table.
example.fact: 碰 is a common everyday verb for accidentally bumping or touching something, often used as a warning like this one.

meanings: (bound form) boat; craft (esp. small or naval)

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 艇 names a small boat or craft.
廷 (tíng) gives a sound very close to tǐng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: They took a small boat to the island.
example.fact: 艇 usually appears in compounds for specific small craft, like 潜艇 (qiántǐng, 'submarine') and 游艇 (yóutǐng, 'yacht').

etymologyHint: Resembling 肖 grain 禾; 肖 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稍 relates to a small amount of grain.
肖 (to resemble) — grain 禾 that only resembles a full harvest, a slightly smaller amount, gave 稍 its meaning 'slightly, a little.'

example.english: Please wait a moment.
example.fact: 稍 almost always appears in 稍等 (shāo děng, 'please wait a moment') and 稍微 (shāowēi, 'slightly').

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 迟 describes moving too slowly, arriving 'late.'
尺 (chǐ) gives a sound very close to chí, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: Sorry, I came late.
example.fact: 迟 is the standard word for being late, whether for a meeting, class, or simply arriving after everyone else.

etymologyHint: Two 两 carts 车; 两 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辆 is used to count vehicles, one cart at a time.
两 (two) — its use here, counting out two carts, is the visual root of 辆's job as a measure word for vehicles.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng liàng zìxíngchē.
example.english: My family has two bicycles.
example.fact: 辆 is the measure word used specifically for wheeled vehicles like cars, bikes, and trucks.

components.note: 发 (fā) gives a sound related to fèi, sharing the initial f-, though the rhyme has drifted from ā to èi over time.

example.english: This rule has already been abolished.
example.fact: 废 mainly appears in formal or written contexts, as in 废除 ('to abolish') and 废话 ('nonsense, useless talk').

components.note: 冫 (water/ice) — 净 relates to washing something clean and pure.
争 (zhēng) is only distantly related in sound to jìng — both end in a nasal final, but the initial and exact rhyme have drifted apart.

example.english: Please wipe the table clean.
example.fact: 净 most often appears in 干净 (gānjìng, 'clean'), one of the first adjectives beginners learn for tidiness.

etymologyHint: A container 凵 of wickedness 乂

components.note: 凵 depicts an open container or pit, shown here holding something dangerous inside.
乂 is a crossed mark suggesting something tangled or harmful — trapped inside the container 凵, it gives 凶 its meaning 'vicious, ominous.'

example.pinyin: Nà zhī gǒu kàn qǐlái hěn xiōng.
example.english: That dog looks fierce.
example.fact: 凶 describes something fierce or ominous, and often appears in 凶手 (xiōngshǒu), the word for a murderer or culprit.

components.note: 罒 (net) — 署 originally related to an official's net of duties or jurisdiction, giving 'office, bureau.'
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to shǔ's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He works at the police station.
example.fact: 署 usually names a government office or bureau, as in 警察署 ('police station') or 办公署 ('administrative office').

components.note: 土 (earth) — 壁 describes a wall, often built of earth or clay.
辟 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 壁.

example.pinyin: Qiángbì shàng guàzhe yì fú huà.
example.english: A painting hangs on the wall.
example.fact: 壁 almost always appears together with 墙 in 墙壁 (qiángbì, 'wall'), rather than standing alone.

components.note: 彳 (step, movement) — 御 relates to travel, as in driving or riding a chariot.
卸 (xiè) gives a sound distantly related to yù's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Ancient emperors had carriages for their own use.
example.fact: 御 today survives mainly in formal or historical words like 御用 ('for the emperor's/official use') and 防御 ('defense').

example.hanzi: 他为学校奉献了很多时间。
example.pinyin: Tā wèi xuéxiào fèngxiànle hěn duō shíjiān.
example.english: He devoted a lot of time to the school.
example.fact: 奉 is a formal word for offering something respectfully, most often seen in 奉献 (fèngxiàn, 'to dedicate, to offer').

etymologyHint: An army 方 marching under a flag 疋

components.note: 方 here depicts a banner or flag flying from a pole, marking where troops are gathered.
疋 depicts a pair of marching feet — moving beneath the flag 方, the image gave 旋 its meaning 'to circle around, to return.'

example.english: The Earth revolves around the sun.
example.fact: 旋 most commonly appears in 旋转 (xuánzhuǎn, 'to rotate, to revolve'), a basic science word for circular motion.

etymologyHint: A man walking 夂 on ice ⺀

components.note: 夂 depicts a foot trailing behind, the image of a person trudging slowly forward.
⺀ depicts two small drops standing for ice — combined with the trudging foot 夂, it pictures walking through the cold, giving 冬 its meaning 'winter.'

example.pinyin: Dōngtiān hěn lěng, yào duō chuān yīfu.
example.english: Winter is very cold, you need to wear more clothes.
example.fact: 冬天 (dōngtiān, 'winter') is one of the four seasons every beginner learns early in Mandarin study.

components.note: 石 (rock/stone) — 矿 names a mineral deposit dug out of rock.
广 (guǎng) shares the rhyme -uang with kuàng, and both use a velar initial (g/k) — only the aspiration and tone differ.

example.english: This place has an iron mine.
example.fact: 矿 appears in words for specific minerals and mining, like 铁矿 (tiěkuàng, 'iron ore') and 矿泉水 (kuàngquánshuǐ, 'mineral water').

meanings: (of two or more persons) to carry

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抬 describes lifting or carrying something by hand.
台 (tái) gives the sound — an exact match with 抬.

example.hanzi: 他们一起把桌子抬起来。
example.pinyin: Tāmen yìqǐ bǎ zhuōzi tái qǐlái.
example.english: They lifted the table together.
example.fact: 抬 is the everyday verb for lifting something, especially heavy items that need two or more people, as in 抬桌子.

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — 蛋 names an egg, historically grouped together with small creatures like insects and reptiles.
延 (yán) is only distantly related in sound to dàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.english: Mom boils eggs every morning.
example.fact: 鸡蛋 (jīdàn, 'chicken egg') is one of the first food words beginners learn, and 蛋 also names other round objects like 脸蛋 ('face').

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晨 describes the time when the sun first rises, 'early morning.'
辰 (chén) gives the sound — an exact match with 晨.

example.english: He likes to jog in the early morning.
example.fact: 晨 usually appears in 早晨 (zǎochén) and 清晨 (qīngchén), both meaning 'early morning,' rather than standing alone.

etymologyHint: A person 亻 acting like a dog 犬

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伏 describes a person's posture, crouched low to the ground.
犬 (dog) — paired with the person 亻, the image of someone lying low like a dog gave 伏 its meaning 'to crouch, to lie hidden.'

example.pinyin: Shìbīng fú zài dì shàng děngdài.
example.english: The soldier lay low on the ground, waiting.
example.fact: 伏 describes crouching or lying low, and appears in words like 埋伏 (máifú, 'to ambush') and 伏天 (fútiān, the hottest days of summer).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吹 describes blowing air out of the mouth.
欠 (qiàn) is only distantly related in sound to chuī — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Wàimiàn fēng hěn dà, yìzhí zài chuī.
example.english: It's very windy outside, it keeps blowing.
example.fact: 吹 is the everyday verb for blowing, whether it's the wind, a whistle, or a musical instrument.

etymologyHint: Another 又 kind of bird 鸟

components.note: 又 (hand, here standing in for 奚, part of the original character) — a simplified stroke that no longer pictures anything on its own.
鸟 (bird) — combined with the simplified left side, 鸡 names a specific 'kind of bird,' the chicken.

example.pinyin: Nóngcūn lǐ yǎngle hěn duō jī.
example.english: The village raises a lot of chickens.
example.fact: 鸡 is one of the most common farm-animal words in Mandarin, and also appears in the dish name 鸡蛋 ('chicken egg') and the zodiac sign 鸡年 ('Year of the Rooster').

example.hanzi: 这个价格是原来的三倍。
example.pinyin: Zhège jiàgé shì yuánlái de sān bèi.
example.english: This price is three times the original.
example.fact: 倍 is the standard word for multiples, always following a number, as in 两倍 ('double') or 三倍 ('triple').

components.note: 米 (grain/rice) — 糊 originally referred to a paste made from rice or grain.
胡 (hú) gives the sound — an exact match with 糊.

example.pinyin: Bǎ zhèxiē cáiliào hú zài qiáng shàng.
example.english: Paste these materials onto the wall.
example.fact: 糊 names a sticky paste and also describes something blurry or muddled, as in 糊涂 (hútu, 'confused').

meanings: short name for 陝西|陕西[Shan3 xi1]

example.hanzi: 秦是中国历史上的一个朝代。
example.pinyin: Qín shì Zhōngguó lìshǐ shàng de yí gè cháodài.
example.english: Qin is a dynasty in Chinese history.
example.fact: 秦 is best known as the name of China's first unified dynasty, the Qin Dynasty, and today survives mainly as a surname.

etymologyHint: An eye 目 peering from behind a shield 厂

components.note: 厂 depicts a slanted overhang, here standing for a protective shield.
目 (eye) — an eye peering out from behind the shield 厂 gives 盾 its meaning 'shield.'

example.hanzi: 古代士兵用盾保护自己。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài shìbīng yòng dùn bǎohù zìjǐ.
example.english: Ancient soldiers used shields to protect themselves.
example.fact: 盾 names a shield, and also appears in the word 矛盾 (máodùn, 'contradiction'), literally 'spear and shield.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — 杯 names a cup, originally carved from wood.
不 (bù) shares the initial b- with bēi, though the rhyme has drifted from ù to ēi over time.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi shuǐ.
example.english: Please give me a glass of water.
example.fact: 杯 names a cup or glass, and also serves as the measure word for drinks, as in 一杯水 ('a glass of water').

etymologyHint: Regularly paid 且 tribute in grain 禾

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 租 originally described tribute paid in grain.
且 here marks the payment as regular and ongoing — combined with the grain 禾, it gave 租 its meaning 'rent, tax.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen měi gè yuè fù fángzū.
example.english: We pay rent every month.
example.fact: 租 is the everyday word for rent, most often seen in 房租 (fángzū, 'house rent') and 租车 (zūchē, 'to rent a car').

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骑 describes riding on horseback.
奇 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 骑.

example.english: He rides his bicycle to work every day.
example.fact: 骑 is the everyday verb for riding something you straddle, like a bike, motorcycle, or horse.

etymologyHint: A foot 之 running into a wall or barrier 丿

components.note: 之 depicts a foot stepping forward.
丿 marks a barrier in front of the foot — a step blocked by a wall gave 乏 its meaning 'lacking, tired.'

example.english: He feels exhausted.
example.fact: 乏 rarely stands alone today, mostly appearing in words like 疲乏 (pífá, 'tired, worn out') and 缺乏 (quēfá, 'to lack').

meanings: short for 吉隆坡[Ji2 long2 po1], Kuala Lumpur

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā fànguǎn shēngyì hěn xīnglóng.
example.english: This restaurant's business is thriving.
example.fact: 隆 mostly appears in words describing prosperity, like 兴隆 (xīnglóng, 'flourishing') and 隆重 (lóngzhòng, 'grand, ceremonious').

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诊 describes a doctor asking questions and speaking with a patient to diagnose an illness.
㐱 (zhěn) gives the sound — an exact match with 诊.

example.english: The doctor is examining the patient.
example.fact: 诊 is a medical word appearing in 诊断 (zhěnduàn, 'to diagnose') and 门诊 (ménzhěn, 'outpatient clinic').

etymologyHint: A woman 女 standing by her master's right hand 又; 女 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 (woman) — 奴 originally described a woman kept as a servant in a household.
又 (a hand) — standing beside the master's hand 又, the woman 女 gave 奴 its meaning 'slave, servant.'

example.pinyin: Zài gǔdài, hěn duō rén shì núlì.
example.english: In ancient times, many people were slaves.
example.fact: 奴 almost always appears in 奴隶 (núlì, 'slave'), a word describing a difficult period of history.

meanings: (bound form) to take in; to absorb; to assimilate

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摄 describes taking hold of or capturing something, as in taking a photograph.
聂 (niè) gives a sound distantly related to shè's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He likes to take photos with his phone.
example.fact: 摄 most often appears in 摄影 (shèyǐng, 'photography') and 摄像头 (shèxiàngtóu, 'camera lens').

meanings: to be bereaved of (one's spouse etc)
etymologyHint: Simplified form of 喪; to cry 哭 over the dead 亡

components.note: 哭 (to cry) — the top of the simplified character keeps the idea of crying in mourning.
亡 (dead, gone) — combined with crying above it, the image of weeping over the dead gave 丧 its meaning 'mourning, funeral.'

example.pinyin: Tā zài wèi qīnrén bàn sāngshì.
example.english: He is arranging a funeral for a relative.
example.fact: 丧 mostly appears in formal words about death and mourning, like 丧事 (sāngshì, 'funeral matters').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 污 describes water, or anything else, that has become dirty or polluted.
亏 (kuī) is only distantly related in sound to wū — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo hé de shuǐ bèi wūrǎn le.
example.english: This river's water has been polluted.
example.fact: 污 is almost always paired with 染 in 污染 (wūrǎn, 'to pollute'), a common word in discussions about the environment.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渡 describes crossing over a body of water.
度 (dù) gives the sound — an exact match with 渡.

example.hanzi: 他们坐船渡过了这条河。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zuò chuán dùguò le zhè tiáo hé.
example.english: They crossed this river by boat.
example.fact: 渡 is the classic verb for crossing water by boat or ferry, and appears in 渡船 (dùchuán, 'ferry').

meanings: (in Qing times) Manchu (cf. 八旗[Ba1 qi2])

components.note: 方 (here, a flagpole with streamers) — 旗 names a flag or banner flown from a pole.
其 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 旗.

example.english: The national flag flutters in the wind.
example.fact: 旗 most commonly appears in 国旗 (guóqí, 'national flag'), one of the first symbols of a country that students learn.

meanings: short name for Gansu 甘肅|甘肃[Gan1 su4]
etymologyHint: Picture of a tongue with 一 marking the sweet spot

example.english: This fruit is very sweet.
example.fact: 甘 is a literary word for 'sweet,' most often seen today in compounds like 甘甜 (gāntián, 'sweet') rather than alone.

meanings: (bound form) to bear; to endure; to withstand

example.english: This material is very durable.
example.fact: 耐 usually appears in compounds like 耐用 (nàiyòng, 'durable') and 耐心 (nàixīn, 'patience'), describing the ability to withstand or endure something.

etymologyHint: Leaning on (trusting) 任 a table 几

components.note: 任 (to trust, to bear) — 凭 describes trusting or relying on something.
几 (a small table) — leaning on a table for support pictures what it feels like to depend on something, giving 凭 its meaning 'to rely on.'

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì bù néng guāng píng cāicè.
example.english: This matter cannot rely only on guesswork.
example.fact: 凭 means 'to rely on' or 'based on,' and often appears in the phrase 凭什么 (píng shénme, 'on what basis, why should').

meanings: to run or stick (a needle etc) into
used in 掙扎|挣扎[zheng1 zha2]
etymologyHint: A hand 扌 tying a bundle with string 乚

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扎 describes a hand at work tying or binding something.
乚 depicts a bent length of string or cord — bound by the hand 扌, it gave 扎 its meaning 'to tie, to bundle.'

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ tóufa zhā qǐlái le.
example.english: She tied her hair up.
example.fact: 扎 is the everyday verb for tying something up, as in 扎头发 ('to tie up one's hair') or 扎辫子 ('to braid').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抢 describes seizing or grabbing something forcefully.
仓 (cāng) is only distantly related in sound to qiǎng — both end in the -ang family, but the initial and tone have drifted apart.

example.english: The thief grabbed her wallet.
example.fact: 抢 describes forcefully grabbing or robbing something, and also appears in 抢购 (qiǎnggòu, 'to rush to buy').

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绪 originally meant the end of a thread, extending to 'clue, beginnings.'
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to xù's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān qíngxù bú tài hǎo.
example.english: He's not in a good mood today.
example.fact: 绪 almost always appears in 情绪 (qíngxù, 'mood, emotion') and 头绪 (tóuxù, 'a clue, a thread of thought').

components.note: 米 (grain) — 粗 originally described coarsely hulled grain, extending to 'rough, coarse' in general.
且 (qiě) gives a sound distantly related to cū's reading, having drifted apart considerably over time.

example.english: This rope is very thick.
example.fact: 粗 describes something thick or coarse, the opposite of 细 (xì, 'thin, fine'), and often describes ropes, lines, or manners.

etymologyHint: A man bringing home meat ⺼ for the family 户

components.note: 户 (door, household) — 肩 relates to a family member returning home.
⺼ (flesh/body) — meat carried home over one's 肩 (shoulder) gave the character its meaning.

example.english: His shoulders are broad.
example.fact: 肩 names the shoulder, and appears in 肩膀 (jiānbǎng, 'shoulder') and idioms about taking on responsibility.

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 bridge built 刅 over a river 氵

components.note: 木 (wood/tree) — 梁 describes a wooden structure, such as a beam or a bridge.
氵 (water/river) — the wooden structure 木 crosses over a river, giving 梁 its original meaning 'bridge,' later extended to 'beam, rafter.'

example.english: The roof beam is broken.
example.fact: 梁 names a beam or rafter holding up a roof, and also appears in 桥梁 (qiáoliáng, 'bridge').

components.note: 予 (to give) — 幻 is drawn as an inverted, mirror-image form of 予, picturing something turned upside down or not as it seems, giving 幻 its meaning 'illusion, fantasy.'

example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng chōngmǎn le huànxiǎng.
example.english: This movie is full of fantasy.
example.fact: 幻 almost always appears in words like 幻想 (huànxiǎng, 'fantasy') and 科幻 (kēhuàn, 'science fiction').

meanings: abbr. for the Philippines 菲律賓|菲律宾[Fei1 lu:4 bin1]

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 菲 describes a richly fragrant, luxuriant plant.
非 (fēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 菲.

example.english: He went to travel in the Philippines.
example.fact: 菲 today is used mostly as the character for 菲律宾 (Fēilǜbīn, 'the Philippines') rather than for its original meaning 'fragrant.'

example.english: All the classmates have already arrived.
example.fact: 皆 is a literary word meaning 'all, every,' more common in written Chinese than in everyday spoken conversation.

components.note: 石 (rock) — 碎 describes something, often stone-like, broken into pieces.
卒 (zú) is only distantly related in sound to suì — the connection has drifted apart considerably over time.

example.pinyin: Bēizi diào zài dì shàng suì le.
example.english: The cup fell on the ground and shattered.
example.fact: 碎 describes something breaking into small pieces, and also appears in 破碎 (pòsuì, 'broken, shattered').

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宙 extends the idea of a roof overhead to the vastness of time and space, 'the universe.'
由 (yóu) shares the rhyme -ou with zhòu, though the initial has drifted from y- to zh- over time.

example.english: The universe is extremely big.
example.fact: 宙 almost never stands alone, appearing instead in 宇宙 (yǔzhòu, 'the universe'), pairing space (宇) with time (宙).

components.note: 小 (small, young) — 叔 describes a younger member of the family.
又 (a hand) — historically part of a scene of picking beans; today it simply combines with 小 to give 叔 its meaning 'a younger uncle.'

example.english: This is my uncle.
example.fact: 叔叔 (shūshu) specifically means a father's younger brother, showing how Chinese kinship terms are more precise than the single English word 'uncle.'

etymologyHint: The rocks 石 that make up a mountain 山

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 岩 names the rock that makes up a mountain.
石 (rock/stone) — together with 山, the image of rock forming a mountain gave 岩 its meaning 'cliff, rock.'

example.english: Be careful of the rocks when climbing the mountain.
example.fact: 岩 almost always appears in 岩石 (yánshí, 'rock') and 火山岩 (huǒshānyán, 'volcanic rock').

etymologyHint: Hot water 汤 wiping out plant life 艹; 汤 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 汤 depicts hot water — its heat is strong enough to wipe out whatever it touches.
艹 (plant) — hot water 汤 wiping out plant life gave 荡 its meaning 'to wash away, to sweep clean.'

example.english: The water sways back and forth.
example.fact: 荡 describes swaying or sweeping motion, and appears in 动荡 (dòngdàng, 'turmoil, instability') and 荡秋千 (dàng qiūqiān, 'to swing on a swing').

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 综 originally described the heddle threads on a loom, extending to 'weave together, combine.'
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 综.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí fèn zōnghé bàogào.
example.english: This is a comprehensive report.
example.fact: 综 almost always appears in 综合 (zōnghé, 'comprehensive, synthesized'), a common word in schoolwork and reports.

components.note: 爪 (claw) — 爬 describes crawling or climbing using claws, or hands and feet.
巴 (bā) shares the rhyme -a and a related bilabial initial (b/p) with pá, just the tone differs.

example.english: The kitten is climbing the tree.
example.fact: 爬 is the everyday verb for climbing or crawling, used for babies crawling, cats climbing trees, or people climbing mountains.

meanings: to carry on one's shoulder or back

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 荷 names the lotus plant.
何 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match with 荷.

example.english: The pond is full of blooming lotus flowers.
example.fact: 荷 mostly appears in 荷花 (héhuā, 'lotus flower'), a plant with deep cultural meaning in China, often linked to purity.

components.note: 心 (mind) — 悉 describes coming to fully know or understand something in one's mind.
釆 (biàn) is only distantly related in sound to xī — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.hanzi: 我对这个情况不太熟悉。
example.pinyin: Wǒ duì zhège qíngkuàng bú tài shúxī.
example.english: I'm not very familiar with this situation.
example.fact: 悉 almost always appears in 熟悉 (shúxī, 'to be familiar with'), a common word for knowing something well.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蒂 names the stem that attaches a fruit or flower to its plant.
帝 (dì) gives the sound — an exact match with 蒂.

example.pinyin: Píngguǒ de dì hái zài shàngmiàn.
example.english: The apple's stem is still on it.
example.fact: 蒂 names the small stem connecting a fruit to its branch, and appears in the idiom 根深蒂固 (gēnshēndìgù, 'deeply rooted').

etymologyHint: To walk 辶 backwards 反; 反 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 返 describes the act of traveling.
反 (opposite, reversed) — walking 辶 in reverse 反 gave 返 its meaning 'to return.'

example.english: He is returning to his hometown tomorrow.
example.fact: 返 usually appears in formal travel words like 返回 (fǎnhuí, 'to return') and 往返 (wǎngfǎn, 'round trip').

components.note: 井 is a simplified picture of a wooden frame built around the mouth of a well, seen from above.

example.pinyin: Cūn lǐ yǒu yì kǒu lǎo jǐng.
example.english: There is an old well in the village.
example.fact: 井 names a well, and 口 is the special measure word used to count wells, as in 一口井.

components.note: 士 (soldier) — 壮 describes someone as strong and robust, like a sturdy soldier.
丬 is only distantly related in sound to zhuàng — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.english: This young man is very sturdy.
example.fact: 壮 describes physical strength and robustness, and also appears in 强壮 (qiángzhuàng, 'strong, robust').

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 薄 originally described sparse, thin grass, extending to 'thin' in general.
溥 (pǔ) is only distantly related in sound to báo — the rhyme has drifted apart over time.

example.english: This book is very thin.
example.fact: 薄 describes something thin, the opposite of 厚 (hòu, 'thick'), and is used for books, paper, and clothing.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 悄 describes a quiet, anxious inner feeling.
肖 (xiào) shares the rhyme -iao with qiāo, and both come from the same historical initial series (q/x) — only the specific initial and tone differ.

example.english: He quietly walked into the room.
example.fact: 悄 almost always appears doubled as 悄悄 (qiāoqiāo, 'quietly, secretly'), describing doing something without being noticed.

meanings: to sweep (with a brush or broom)
to sweep away; to wipe out; to get rid of
to sweep (one's eyes etc) over; to scan
etymologyHint: Simplified form of 掃; to use 扌 a broom 帚; 帚 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扫 describes using the hand to sweep.
帚 depicts a hand-held broom — held by the hand 扌, it gave 扫 its meaning 'to sweep.'

example.english: She sweeps the floor every morning.
example.fact: 扫 is the everyday verb for sweeping, most often seen in 扫地 (sǎodì, 'to sweep the floor').

components.note: 攵 (to act, strike) — 敏 describes being quick and effective in action, 'nimble, sharp.'
每 (měi) is only distantly related in sound to mǐn — the rhyme has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī māo de dòngzuò hěn mǐnjié.
example.english: This cat's movements are very agile.
example.fact: 敏 almost always appears in 敏捷 (mǐnjié, 'agile, quick') and 敏感 (mǐngǎn, 'sensitive').

components.note: 石 (stone) — 碍 describes something solid, like a stone, blocking one's path.
㝵 gives a sound closely related to ài, though pronunciation has drifted somewhat over time.

example.english: There is an obstacle on the road.
example.fact: 碍 almost always appears in 障碍 (zhàng'ài, 'obstacle') and 妨碍 (fáng'ài, 'to hinder').

components.note: 歹 (bones/remains) — 殖 originally related to accumulated remains, extending to 'to grow, to breed.'
直 (zhí) gives the sound — an exact match with 殖.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yú fánzhí de hěn kuài.
example.english: This kind of fish breeds very quickly.
example.fact: 殖 almost always appears in 繁殖 (fánzhí, 'to breed, to reproduce') and 殖民 (zhímín, 'to colonize').

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 详 describes speech or an account that is thorough and detailed.
羊 (yáng) shares the rhyme family -ang with xiáng, though the initial has drifted from y- to x- over time.

example.hanzi: 请详细介绍一下你自己。
example.pinyin: Qǐng xiángxì jièshào yíxià nǐ zìjǐ.
example.english: Please introduce yourself in detail.
example.fact: 详 almost always appears in 详细 (xiángxì, 'detailed'), a common word when asking for or giving more information.

etymologyHint: To walk 辶 with purpose 由

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 迪 describes moving forward.
由 (a source, a path from) — walking 辶 from a clear starting point 由 gave 迪 its meaning 'to guide, to enlighten.'

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū hěn yǒu qǐdí yìyì.
example.english: This book is very enlightening.
example.fact: 迪 mostly appears in the formal word 启迪 (qǐdí, 'to enlighten, to inspire') and as a common sound in transliterated names.

etymologyHint: A spear pointed up and to the right

components.note: 矛 is a simplified picture of a long spear, its point aimed up and to the right.

example.english: Ancient soldiers fought with spears.
example.fact: 矛 names a spear, and also appears in the idiom 矛盾 (máodùn, 'contradiction'), literally 'spear and shield.'

etymologyHint: Birds 隹 caught in a sudden storm 雨

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霍 pictures a sudden downpour.
隹 (a short-tailed bird) — birds startled and scattered by a sudden storm of rain 雨 gave 霍 its meaning 'suddenly, quickly.'

example.pinyin: Tā huò de zhàn le qǐlái.
example.english: He suddenly stood up.
example.fact: 霍 describes a sudden, quick motion, most often seen in the adverb 霍地 (huò de, 'suddenly') and as a surname.

example.hanzi: 老师允许我们提前离开。
example.english: The teacher allowed us to leave early.
example.fact: 允 almost always appears in 允许 (yǔnxǔ, 'to permit, to allow'), a common word for granting permission.

etymologyHint: A roll 畐 of cloth 巾; 畐 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 幅 measures a length of cloth.
畐 depicts a full, rounded container — the sense of a full, rolled-out width of cloth gave 幅 its meaning 'width, a roll of cloth.'

example.pinyin: Qiáng shàng guàzhe yì fú huà.
example.english: A painting hangs on the wall.
example.fact: 幅 is the measure word for flat things like paintings and pieces of cloth, as in 一幅画 ('a painting').

etymologyHint: To scatter 散 seeds by hand 扌; 散 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撒 describes scattering something by hand.
散 (to scatter, to disperse) — combined with the hand 扌, it gave 撒 its meaning 'to scatter, to release.'

example.pinyin: Nóngmín zài dì lǐ sā zhǒngzi.
example.english: The farmer scatters seeds in the field.
example.fact: 撒 is the everyday verb for scattering or sprinkling something, as in 撒种子 ('to sow seeds') and 撒盐 ('to sprinkle salt').

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剩 originally involved cutting away a surplus portion, giving 'to remain, leftover.'
乘 (chéng) shares the rhyme -eng and a related retroflex initial (ch/sh) with shèng — only the tone differs.

example.english: There is still some rice left over.
example.fact: 剩 describes what remains or is left over, most often seen in 剩下 (shèngxià, 'to remain') and 剩饭 ('leftover food').

example.english: The athletes returned home in triumph.
example.fact: 凯 is a formal word for victory, almost always appearing in 凯旋 (kǎixuán, 'to return in triumph').

components.note: 果 (a round, fruit-like shape) — 颗 is used to count small round things like grains or pearls.
页 (yè) gives a sound distantly related to kē's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Zhuō shàng yǒu yì kē táng.
example.english: There is a piece of candy on the table.
example.fact: 颗 is the measure word for small round objects, like 一颗糖 ('a piece of candy') or 一颗星 ('a star').

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 骂 describes shouting angry words from the mouth, 'to scold.'
马 (mǎ) gives a sound very close to mà, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: Mom scolded younger brother with a word.
example.fact: 骂 is the everyday verb for scolding or cursing someone, often used when talking about being told off by a parent.

components.note: 贝 (money) — 赏 describes giving money or valuables as a reward.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound very close to shǎng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.hanzi: 老师奖赏了努力的学生。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī jiǎngshǎng le nǔlì de xuéshēng.
example.english: The teacher rewarded the hard-working student.
example.fact: 赏 means to bestow a reward, and appears in 奖赏 (jiǎngshǎng, 'to reward') and 欣赏 (xīnshǎng, 'to appreciate').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 液 names any liquid or fluid.
夜 (yè) gives the sound — an exact match with 液.

example.english: Blood flows through the body.
example.fact: 液 almost always appears in 血液 (xiěyè, 'blood') and 液体 (yètǐ, 'liquid'), both common science words.

etymologyHint: Sowing seeds 米 on the farm 田

components.note: 米 (grain) — 番 pictures seeds scattered by hand.
田 (a farm field) — seeds 米 sown onto a field 田 gave 番 its meaning 'a turn, a time' — as one crop follows another in turn.

example.english: He put in quite some effort.
example.fact: 番 is a formal measure word for 'a certain amount, a turn,' most often seen in the set phrase 一番 (yì fān, 'quite a bit of').

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 箱 originally described a bamboo case or chest.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 箱.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yīfu fàng jìn xiāngzi lǐ.
example.english: He put the clothes into the box.
example.fact: 箱 names a box or case, and appears in 箱子 (xiāngzi, 'box, case') and 冰箱 (bīngxiāng, 'refrigerator').

components.note: 贝 (money) — 贴 originally referred to pawning something for money, extending to 'to stick on, to subsidize.'
占 (zhàn) is only distantly related in sound to tiē — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ zhàopiàn tiē zài qiáng shàng.
example.english: She stuck the photo on the wall.
example.fact: 贴 is the everyday verb for sticking or pasting something on, as in 贴照片 ('to put up a photo') and 贴纸 (tiēzhǐ, 'sticker').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 漫 describes water overflowing and spreading everywhere.
曼 (màn) gives the sound — an exact match with 漫.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢漫无目的地散步。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan mànwú mùdì de sànbù.
example.english: He likes to wander around aimlessly.
example.fact: 漫 describes something spreading freely without limit, as in 漫画 (mànhuà, 'comics') and 浪漫 (làngmàn, 'romantic').

etymologyHint: Wine 酉 aged too long 夋; 夋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 酉 depicts a wine jar — 酸 relates to fermented drink.
夋 here marks the wine as aged for a long time — wine left too long turns sour, giving 酸 its meaning 'sour, acidic.'

example.english: This orange is very sour.
example.fact: 酸 describes a sour taste, and also names the science word 酸 ('acid'), as in 柠檬很酸 ('lemons are very sour').

etymologyHint: A man from a good 良 place 阝;  良 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 良 (good) — 郎 originally described a fine, well-regarded man.
阝 (a settlement, a place) — a good man 良 from a certain place 阝 gave 郎 its meaning 'a young man, a gentleman.'

example.english: The groom is very happy today.
example.fact: 郎 mostly appears today in 新郎 (xīnláng, 'groom') and as part of names, rather than as a standalone word.

meanings: (bound form) kidney of an animal (as food)
the waist of trousers or a skirt

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 腰 names the waist, a part of the body.
要 (yào) gives a sound very close to yāo, sharing the rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: His waist hurts a little.
example.fact: 腰 names the waist, and appears in 腰带 (yāodài, 'belt') and 弯腰 (wānyāo, 'to bend down').

components.note: 舍 (house) — 舒 relates to a sense of settled, at-ease comfort, 'relaxed, comfortable.'
予 (yǔ) is only distantly related in sound to shū — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tǎng zài chuáng shàng hěn shūfu.
example.english: Lying on the bed feels very comfortable.
example.fact: 舒 almost always appears in 舒服 (shūfu, 'comfortable'), one of the first adjectives beginners learn for physical comfort.

etymologyHint: Picture of hair 尸 above an eye 目

components.note: 尸 here stands in for hair or a brow ridge, sitting above the eye.
目 (eye) — with hair pictured above it, the image gave 眉 its meaning 'eyebrow.'

example.english: Her eyebrows are very pretty.
example.fact: 眉 names the eyebrow, and appears in 眉毛 (méimao, 'eyebrow') and the idiom 愁眉 ('a worried brow').

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 忧 describes a heart or mind troubled by worry.
尤 (yóu) gives a sound very close to yōu, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.pinyin: Māma hěn dānyōu wǒ de jiànkāng.
example.english: Mom worries a lot about my health.
example.fact: 忧 means 'to worry,' and appears in 担忧 (dānyōu, 'to worry about') and 忧郁 (yōuyù, 'melancholy').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浮 describes something floating on water.
孚 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 浮.

example.english: The boat floats on the surface of the water.
example.fact: 浮 is the everyday verb for floating, and also appears in 浮云 (fúyún, 'floating clouds') and 漂浮 (piāofú, 'to float').

etymologyHint: A hot iron used to brand prisoners and slaves

components.note: 辛 is traditionally read as a picture of a hot branding iron, once used to mark prisoners — a harsh origin behind its meaning 'bitter, laborious.'

example.english: This job is very hard work.
example.fact: 辛 almost always appears in 辛苦 (xīnkǔ, 'hard, toilsome') and 辛辣 (xīnlà, 'spicy, pungent').

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恋 describes a heart drawn to and longing for someone or something.
亦 (yì) is only distantly related in sound to liàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.english: They are in love.
example.fact: 恋 almost always appears in 恋爱 (liàn'ài, 'to be in love') and 失恋 (shīliàn, 'to have a broken heart').

components.note: 食 (food) — 餐 relates directly to eating and meals.

example.hanzi: 我们一起吃了一顿晚餐。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yìqǐ chīle yí dùn wǎncān.
example.english: We had dinner together.
example.fact: 餐 is the formal word for a meal, and 顿 is the measure word used with it, as in 一顿晚餐 ('a dinner').

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吓 relates to a shout or cry, as when someone is frightened.
下 (xià) gives the sound — an exact match with 吓.

example.pinyin: Nà zhī gǒu xiàle wǒ yí tiào.
example.english: That dog gave me a scare.
example.fact: 吓 means 'to scare,' and often appears in the phrase 吓一跳 (xià yí tiào, 'to give someone a fright').

meanings: to stick out (a part of the body)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 挺 describes straightening or holding something upright, often with the hand or body.
廷 (tíng) gives a sound very close to tǐng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: He stood up straight with his chest out.
example.fact: 挺 as a verb means to straighten up, but is also very common as an adverb meaning 'quite, rather,' as in 挺好 ('quite good').

components.note: 力 (strength) — 励 relates to exerting effort or spurring on strength in others, 'to encourage.'
厉 (lì) gives the sound — an exact match with 励.

example.hanzi: 老师鼓励我们努力学习。
example.english: The teacher encourages us to study hard.
example.fact: 励 almost always appears in 鼓励 (gǔlì, 'to encourage') and 奖励 (jiǎnglì, 'to award, to reward').

components.note: 辛 (bitter, harsh) — 辞 describes speech that carries a sharp edge.
舌 (tongue) — bitter 辛 words spoken by the tongue 舌 gave 辞 its meaning 'words, speech,' and later 'to resign, to take leave.'

example.english: He decided to resign and go traveling.
example.fact: 辞 almost always appears in 辞职 (cízhí, 'to resign') and 告辞 (gàocí, 'to take one's leave').

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 艘 is used to count boats and ships.
叟 (sǒu) gives a sound very close to sōu, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.pinyin: Hǎi shàng yǒu jǐ sōu chuán.
example.english: There are a few boats out at sea.
example.fact: 艘 is the measure word specifically for ships and boats, as in 一艘船 ('a boat').

meanings: key (on a piano or computer keyboard)
button (on a mouse or other device)

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 键 originally named a metal bolt or pin, extending to a mechanical 'key.'
建 (jiàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 键.

example.english: Please press this key.
example.fact: 键 names a key on a keyboard or piano, and appears in 关键 (guānjiàn, 'crucial, key') and 键盘 (jiànpán, 'keyboard').

etymologyHint: Five 五 people 亻; 五 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伍 counts out a group of people.
五 (five) — five 五 people 亻 standing together gave 伍 its meaning 'a squad of five, a group.'

example.hanzi: 他曾在部队服役，是队伍中的一员。
example.pinyin: Tā céng zài bùduì fúyì, shì duìwǔ zhōng de yìyuán.
example.english: He once served in the army, as a member of the ranks.
example.fact: 伍 mostly survives today in 队伍 (duìwǔ, 'ranks, troops, procession') and as a surname, rather than standing alone.

meanings: (of a mountain) high and tapered peak or summit

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峰 names the peak or summit of a mountain.
夆 (féng) gives a sound very close to fēng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: That mountain peak is very tall.
example.fact: 峰 names a mountain peak, and also appears figuratively in 高峰 (gāofēng, 'peak, high point') and 巅峰 (diānfēng, 'summit').

etymologyHint: Picture of a man measuring by pacing

components.note: 尺 is traditionally read as a picture of a bent leg taking a measured step, used before rulers existed to pace off a distance — the origin of its meaning 'a Chinese foot, a ruler.'

example.pinyin: Zhè kuài bù cháng sān chǐ.
example.english: This piece of cloth is three chi long.
example.fact: 尺 is a traditional Chinese unit of length, roughly a third of a meter, and also names the tool 尺子 (chǐzi, 'ruler').

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — 昨 relates to a day, specifically the one before today.
乍 (zhà) is only distantly related in sound to zuó — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.english: The weather was very good yesterday.
example.fact: 昨 almost always appears in 昨天 (zuótiān, 'yesterday'), one of the first time words every beginner learns.

meanings: Li ethnic group of Hainan Province

example.pinyin: Límíng qián de tiānkōng hěn àn.
example.english: The sky is very dark before dawn.
example.fact: 黎 mostly appears today in 黎明 (límíng, 'dawn') and as a surname, rather than standing alone.

components.note: 车 (cart) — 辈 originally described a row of chariots traveling together, extending to a 'group, generation' of people.
非 (fēi) gives a sound distantly related to bèi's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: We are people of the same generation.
example.fact: 辈 means 'generation,' and appears in 同辈 (tóngbèi, 'same generation') and 长辈 (zhǎngbèi, 'elders').

components.note: 贝 (money) — 贯 describes a string threading through a set of coins, 'a string of cash.'
毌 (guàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 贯, and is in fact the ancient ancestor character of 贯, already depicting something pierced through on a string.

example.english: He is consistently hardworking.
example.fact: 贯 means 'to pass through consistently,' and appears in 一贯 (yíguàn, 'consistently') and 贯穿 (guànchuān, 'to run through').

components.note: 亻 (person) — 侦 describes a person who investigates or spies.
贞 (zhēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 侦.

example.english: The police are investigating this case.
example.fact: 侦 almost always appears in 侦查 (zhēnchá, 'to investigate') and 侦探 (zhēntàn, 'detective').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 滑 describes something as slick or slippery, like a wet surface.
骨 (gǔ) is only distantly related in sound to huá — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.pinyin: Dì shàng hěn huá, xiǎoxīn shuāidǎo.
example.english: The ground is very slippery, be careful not to fall.
example.fact: 滑 describes something slippery, and also names the sport 滑雪 (huáxuě, 'skiing') and 滑冰 (huábīng, 'ice skating').

components.note: 刀 (knife) — 券 originally described a tally or contract notched with a knife, extending to 'certificate, ticket.'
龹 shares its top shape with 卷/圈, whose reading quàn matches 券 directly.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì zhāng diànyǐng piàoquàn.
example.english: This is a movie ticket voucher.
example.fact: 券 names a ticket or certificate, and appears in 优惠券 (yōuhuìquàn, 'coupon') and 债券 (zhàiquàn, 'bond').

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崇 describes something towering high, like a mountain, extending to 'to revere.'
宗 (zōng) shares the rhyme -ong with chóng, though the initial has drifted from z- to ch- over time.

example.pinyin: Hěn duō rén chóngbài zhè wèi lǎoshī.
example.english: Many people admire this teacher.
example.fact: 崇 almost always appears in 崇拜 (chóngbài, 'to worship, to admire') and 崇高 (chónggāo, 'lofty, noble').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扰 describes stirring something up by hand, 'to disturb.'
尤 (yóu) is only distantly related in sound to rǎo — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.english: Sorry to disturb you for a moment.
example.fact: 扰 almost always appears in 打扰 (dǎrǎo, 'to disturb'), a common polite phrase before interrupting someone.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宪 relates to an overarching structure of rules, as in a nation's 'constitution.'
先 (xiān) gives a sound very close to xiàn, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: The constitution protects citizens' rights.
example.fact: 宪 almost always appears in 宪法 (xiànfǎ, 'constitution'), a formal word for a country's foundational law.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绕 describes winding thread, or anything else, around something.
尧 (yáo) shares the rhyme -ao with rào, though the initial has drifted from y- to r- over time.

example.english: The road winds around the lake.
example.fact: 绕 describes going around something, and also appears in 围绕 (wéirào, 'to revolve around, to surround').

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 趋 describes moving quickly toward something, 'to hasten.'
刍 (chú) shares the rhyme -ū with qū, though the initial has drifted over time.

example.english: The situation is trending toward stability.
example.fact: 趋 means 'to tend toward,' and appears in 趋势 (qūshì, 'trend') and 趋于 (qūyú, 'to tend toward').

components.note: 心 (heart) — 慈 describes a warm, kind-hearted feeling toward others.
兹 (zī) shares the rhyme -i with cí, and both use dental sibilant initials (c/z) — only the aspiration and tone differ.

example.english: Grandma is very kind and loving to the children.
example.fact: 慈 almost always appears in 慈爱 (cí'ài, 'kind and loving') and 慈善 (císhàn, 'charity').

components.note: 夭 depicts a person leaning to one side, arms swinging — here the pose of walking high up on stilts, giving 乔 its meaning 'tall, lofty.'

example.english: His surname is Qiao.
example.fact: 乔 today mostly survives as a common surname and in the word 乔装 (qiáozhuāng, 'to disguise oneself'), rather than standing alone with its original meaning 'tall.'

example.english: I read Chinese books every day.
example.fact: 阅 almost always appears in 阅读 (yuèdú, 'to read') and 阅览 (yuèlǎn, 'to peruse'), both formal reading words.

meanings: see 可汗[ke4 han2], 汗國|汗国[han2 guo2]

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汗 names sweat, a bodily fluid.
干 (gān) shares the rhyme -an with hàn, though the initial has drifted from g- to h- over time.

example.pinyin: Tā pǎobù hòu mǎntóu shì hàn.
example.english: After running, his whole head was covered in sweat.
example.fact: 汗 names sweat, and appears in 出汗 (chūhàn, 'to sweat') and 汗水 (hànshuǐ, 'sweat, hard work').

meanings: classifier for sticks, rods, pencils etc

components.note: 木 (tree) — 枝 names a branch growing from a tree.
支 (zhī) gives the sound — an exact match with 枝.

example.pinyin: Shù shàng yǒu hěn duō zhīyè.
example.english: There are many branches and leaves on the tree.
example.fact: 枝 names a branch, and appears in 树枝 (shùzhī, 'tree branch') and as a measure word for slender things, like 一枝笔 ('a pen').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拖 describes pulling or dragging something by hand.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ xiāngzi tuō dào ménkǒu.
example.english: He dragged the box to the doorway.
example.fact: 拖 is the everyday verb for dragging something, and also appears in 拖延 (tuōyán, 'to delay, to procrastinate').

meanings: abbr. for 墨西哥[Mo4 xi1 ge1], Mexico
etymologyHint: Chalk made from black 黑 earth 土

components.note: 黑 (black) — 墨 describes something dark in color.
土 (earth) — black 黑 earth 土 gave 墨 its meaning 'ink,' a substance traditionally made from soot and clay-like binders.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng máobǐ hé mò xiězì.
example.english: He writes with a brush and ink.
example.fact: 墨 names ink, and is the material used in traditional Chinese calligraphy alongside the brush.

components.note: 办 (to manage, to handle) — 胁 describes exerting control over someone.
⺼ (flesh/body) — controlling 办 another's body ⺼ gave 胁 its meaning 'to threaten, to coerce.'

example.english: He was threatened by someone.
example.fact: 胁 almost always appears in 威胁 (wēixié, 'to threaten') and 胁迫 (xiépò, 'to coerce').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 插 describes inserting or sticking something in by hand.
臿 (chā) gives the sound — an exact match with 插.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ huā chā zài píngzi lǐ.
example.english: She put the flowers into the vase.
example.fact: 插 is the everyday verb for inserting something, as in 插花 ('flower arranging') and 插图 (chātú, 'illustration').

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 箭 names an arrow, traditionally made from a bamboo shaft.
前 (qián) shares the rhyme -ian with jiàn, though the initial has drifted from q- to j- over time.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng gōngjiàn shèzhòng le mùbiāo.
example.english: He hit the target with a bow and arrow.
example.fact: 箭 names an arrow, and always appears with 弓 in 弓箭 (gōngjiàn, 'bow and arrow').

etymologyHint: A sacrifice of meat ⺼ for the past year 昔

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/meat) — 腊 describes meat prepared as a sacrifice or preserved food.
昔 (former times, the past year) — meat ⺼ set aside for a sacrifice at year's end 昔 gave 腊 its meaning 'preserved meat,' and the name of the 12th lunar month.

example.english: Mom made preserved cured meat.
example.fact: 腊 almost always appears in 腊肉 (làròu, 'cured meat') and 腊月 (làyuè, 'the 12th lunar month').

components.note: 米 (grain) — 粉 names a fine powder, originally made by grinding grain.
分 (fēn) gives a sound very close to fěn, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: Mom bought some flour.
example.fact: 粉 names a fine powder, most commonly 面粉 (miànfěn, 'flour'), and also names rice noodles, as in 米粉 (mǐfěn).

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泥 names mud, a mix of earth and water.
尼 (ní) gives the sound — an exact match with 泥.

example.pinyin: Xiàyǔ hòu dì shàng yǒu hěn duō ní.
example.english: After it rains, there is a lot of mud on the ground.
example.fact: 泥 names mud, and appears in 泥土 (nítǔ, 'soil, mud') and 水泥 (shuǐní, 'cement').

meanings: used in 閼氏|阏氏[yan1 zhi1]

components.note: 氏 is traditionally read as a picture of a person bent over — the image behind its meaning 'clan, family name.'

example.english: Excuse me, what is your family name?
example.fact: 氏 almost always appears in 姓氏 (xìngshì, 'surname, family name'), a formal way to ask or talk about someone's last name.

etymologyHint: The sound 彡 of drums 壴

components.note: 壴 depicts a drum set upright on a stand.
彡 depicts wavy lines representing sound radiating outward — sound 彡 coming from a drum 壴 gave 彭 its meaning, now used mainly as a surname.

example.pinyin: Péng shì yí gè chángjiàn de xìng.
example.english: Peng is a common surname.
example.fact: 彭 today functions almost entirely as a surname, though its ancient form pictured the booming sound of a drum.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拔 describes pulling something out by hand.
犮 (bá) gives the sound — an exact match with 拔.

example.english: He pulled out a weed.
example.fact: 拔 is the everyday verb for pulling something out, as in 拔草 ('to pull weeds') and 拔牙 (báyá, 'to pull a tooth').

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骗 originally described swinging up onto a horse, later extended figuratively to 'to trick, to swindle.'
扁 (biǎn) shares the rhyme -ian with piàn, and both use a bilabial initial (b/p) — only voicing and tone differ.

example.english: Be careful, don't get tricked.
example.fact: 骗 is the everyday verb for tricking or swindling someone, and appears in 骗子 (piànzi, 'a con artist').

components.note: 又 here is a simplified stroke standing in for the tail feathers of the original pictograph of a bird, 鳥.
凡 (fán) is only distantly related in sound to fèng — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Fènghuáng shì chuánshuō zhōng de niǎo.
example.english: The phoenix is a legendary bird.
example.fact: 凤 almost always appears in 凤凰 (fènghuáng, 'phoenix'), a mythical bird important in Chinese culture.

components.note: 心 (mind) — 慧 describes a sharp, clear mind, 'intelligent, wise.'
彗 (huì) gives the sound — an exact match with 慧.

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè cōnghuì de xuéshēng.
example.english: She is a bright student.
example.fact: 慧 almost always appears in 智慧 (zhìhuì, 'wisdom') and 聪慧 (cōnghuì, 'intelligent'), both formal words for cleverness.

meanings: abbr. for 媒體|媒体[mei2 ti3], media, esp. news media

components.note: 女 (woman) — 媒 originally described a woman who arranged marriages, 'a matchmaker.'
某 (mǒu) is only distantly related in sound to méi — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 新闻媒体报道了这件事。
example.pinyin: Xīnwén méitǐ bàodào le zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: The news media reported on this matter.
example.fact: 媒 almost always appears in 媒体 (méitǐ, 'media') and 媒人 (méirén, 'matchmaker').

etymologyHint: Common 凡 cloth 巾 ornaments worn by people 亻

components.note: 凡 (common, ordinary) — 佩 describes an everyday accessory.
巾 (cloth) — a common 凡 cloth 巾 ornament worn by a person 亻 gave 佩 its meaning 'to wear (an ornament), to admire.'

example.pinyin: Dàjiā hěn pèifú tā de yǒngqì.
example.english: Everyone admires his courage.
example.fact: 佩 almost always appears in 佩服 (pèifú, 'to admire'), a common word for expressing respect for someone.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 愤 describes a heart filled with anger or resentment.
贲 is only distantly related in sound to fèn — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他对这件事感到很愤怒。
example.pinyin: Tā duì zhè jiàn shì gǎndào hěn fènnù.
example.english: He feels very angry about this matter.
example.fact: 愤 almost always appears in 愤怒 (fènnù, 'anger') and 气愤 (qìfèn, 'indignant').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扑 describes striking or pouncing with the hand.
卜 shares a bilabial initial (b/p) with pū, though the rhyme has drifted from o to ū over time.

example.english: The puppy pounced on the ball.
example.fact: 扑 describes pouncing or lunging at something, and appears in 扑向 (pū xiàng, 'to pounce toward') and 扑克 (pūkè, 'poker cards').

components.note: 齿 (teeth) — 龄 originally estimated a person's or animal's age by counting their teeth.
令 (lìng) gives a sound very close to líng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.pinyin: Qǐngwèn nín de niánlíng shì duōshao?
example.english: May I ask what your age is?
example.fact: 龄 almost always appears in 年龄 (niánlíng, 'age') and 高龄 (gāolíng, 'advanced age').

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驱 describes spurring a horse onward, extending to 'to drive, to expel.'
区 (qū) gives the sound — an exact match with 驱.

example.hanzi: 医生给了我一些驱虫药。
example.english: The doctor gave me some deworming medicine.
example.fact: 驱 means 'to drive away,' and appears in 驱赶 (qūgǎn, 'to drive away') and 驱动 (qūdòng, 'to drive, to power').

etymologyHint: To feel 忄 for the past 昔; 昔 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惜 describes an emotional response felt in the heart.
昔 (the past, former times) — feeling 忄 for the past 昔 gave 惜 its meaning 'to cherish, to regret.'

example.pinyin: Tā hěn zhēnxī zhè cì jīhuì.
example.english: He treasures this opportunity very much.
example.fact: 惜 almost always appears in 珍惜 (zhēnxī, 'to treasure') and 可惜 (kěxī, 'it's a pity').

components.note: 豕 (boar) — 豪 originally described a fierce, bristling boar-like porcupine, extending to 'heroic, grand.'
高 (gāo) shares the rhyme -ao with háo, though the initial has drifted from g- to h- over time.

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè háoshuǎng de rén.
example.english: He is a bold and generous person.
example.fact: 豪 almost always appears in 豪爽 (háoshuǎng, 'bold and generous') and 自豪 (zìháo, 'proud').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掩 describes covering or shutting something with the hand.
奄 (yǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 掩.

example.pinyin: Tā yǎn zhùle zìjǐ de liǎn.
example.english: She covered her own face.
example.fact: 掩 is the verb for covering or concealing something, and appears in 掩护 (yǎnhù, 'to cover, to shield') and 掩盖 (yǎngài, 'to conceal').

etymologyHint: A hand holding two sheafs of grain 禾

components.note: 禾 (grain), doubled here — 兼 pictures two stalks of grain held together.
彐 depicts a hand grasping — a hand 彐 holding two sheafs of grain 禾禾 at once gave 兼 its meaning 'to combine, to hold two things together.'

example.english: He holds two positions at once.
example.fact: 兼 means 'to combine, to hold together,' and often appears in 兼职 (jiānzhí, 'part-time job') and 兼任 (jiānrèn, 'to hold concurrently').

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跃 describes jumping or leaping with the feet.
夭 (yāo) is only distantly related in sound to yuè — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.pinyin: Tā yuèguò le nà tiáo xiǎohé.
example.english: He leapt over that small river.
example.fact: 跃 means 'to leap,' and appears in 跳跃 (tiàoyuè, 'to jump') and 跃进 (yuèjìn, 'to leap forward').

components.note: 尸 is traditionally read as a picture of a person collapsed or bent over — the origin of its meaning 'corpse.'

example.english: The police are examining the body.
example.fact: 尸 almost always appears in 尸体 (shītǐ, 'corpse, body'), and is also the radical found in words like 尾 ('tail') and 屋 ('room').

example.english: The atmosphere in the hall is very solemn and quiet.
example.fact: 肃 is a formal word appearing in 肃静 (sùjìng, 'solemnly quiet') and 严肃 (yánsù, 'serious, solemn').

etymologyHint: A scarf 巾 used to maintain a girl's purity 巾

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 帕 names a small piece of woven cloth.
白 (white, plain) — a plain white cloth 巾 gave 帕 its meaning 'kerchief, scarf.'

example.english: She wiped her tears with a handkerchief.
example.fact: 帕 almost always appears in 手帕 (shǒupà, 'handkerchief') and 头巾 -like head coverings.

meanings: (of a vehicle, horse etc) to go fast; to speed

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驶 originally described a horse running swiftly, extending to 'to drive, to sail.'
史 (shǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 驶.

example.english: The ship is sailing northward.
example.fact: 驶 almost always appears in 行驶 (xíngshǐ, 'to travel, to sail') and 驾驶 (jiàshǐ, 'to drive').

meanings: (bound form) burger (abbr. for 漢堡|汉堡[han4 bao3])
etymologyHint: Earthen 土 walls built for defense 保; 保 also provides the meaning

components.note: 保 (to protect) — 堡 describes a structure built for defense.
土 (earth) — earthen 土 walls built for defense 保 gave 堡 its meaning 'fort, fortress.'

example.hanzi: 山上有一座古老的城堡。
example.pinyin: Shān shàng yǒu yí zuò gǔlǎo de chéngbǎo.
example.english: There is an old castle on the mountain.
example.fact: 堡 almost always appears in 城堡 (chéngbǎo, 'castle') and 汉堡 (hànbǎo, 'hamburger,' a sound-based borrowing).

example.pinyin: Zhè shì dì wǔ jiè yùndònghuì.
example.english: This is the fifth session of the sports meet.
example.fact: 届 is a measure word for a scheduled term or session, as in 第一届 ('the first session') and 本届 ('this term').

components.note: 欠 (an open mouth, as in a sigh or gasp) — 欣 describes an open expression of joy, 'happy, delighted.'
斤 (jīn) shares the rhyme -in with xīn, and both belong to the same historical initial series (j/q/x) — only the specific initial and tone differ.

example.hanzi: 我们欣赏了一场音乐会。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xīnshǎng le yì chǎng yīnyuèhuì.
example.english: We enjoyed a concert.
example.fact: 欣 almost always appears in 欣赏 (xīnshǎng, 'to appreciate, to enjoy') and 欣喜 (xīnxǐ, 'joyful').

meanings: (bound form) act of kindness (from a superior)
(honorific prefix) kind (as in 惠顧|惠顾[hui4 gu4])

components.note: 心 (heart) — 惠 describes kindness or a favor given from the heart.
叀 is only distantly related in sound to huì — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu yǒu yōuhuì jiàgé.
example.english: This piece of clothing has a discounted price.
example.fact: 惠 almost always appears in 优惠 (yōuhuì, 'discount, preferential') and 恩惠 (ēnhuì, 'favor, kindness').

etymologyHint: Bamboo strips 冂 tied together to form a book

components.note: 册 is a simplified picture of narrow bamboo strips bound together side by side with a cord, the earliest form of a book in China.

example.english: This handbook is very useful.
example.fact: 册 names a booklet or volume, and appears in 手册 (shǒucè, 'handbook') and as a measure word, as in 一册书 ('a volume of a book').

components.note: 亻 (person) — 储 describes a person setting something aside, 'to store, to save.'
诸 (zhū) shares the rhyme -ū with chǔ, and both use retroflex initials (ch/zh) — only the tone differs.

example.hanzi: 他把钱存在储蓄账户里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ qián cún zài chǔxù zhànghù lǐ.
example.english: He deposits the money into a savings account.
example.fact: 储 almost always appears in 储蓄 (chǔxù, 'savings') and 储存 (chǔcún, 'to store').

meanings: to float (in the air); to flutter; to waft

components.note: 风 (wind) — 飘 describes something fluttering or floating on the wind.
票 (piào) gives a sound very close to piāo, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: Leaves flutter down in the wind.
example.fact: 飘 describes something drifting lightly on the air, and appears in 飘落 (piāoluò, 'to flutter down') and 飘扬 (piāoyáng, 'to wave, to flutter').

etymologyHint: A tree 木 bearing berries 叒

components.note: 木 (tree) — 桑 names the mulberry tree.
叒 depicts clusters of leaves or berries — clustered on the tree 木, they gave 桑 its meaning 'mulberry tree.'

example.english: Mulberry leaves are the food of silkworms.
example.fact: 桑 names the mulberry tree, historically important in China for feeding silkworms in silk production.

etymologyHint: A wooden fence 木 with a door 门

components.note: 门 (door, gate) — 闲 describes a fenced-in, quiet space.
木 (wood) — a wooden 木 fence with a door 门 pictures an enclosed, peaceful space, giving 闲 its meaning 'idle, at leisure.'

example.english: I'm relatively free on the weekend.
example.fact: 闲 means 'free, idle,' and appears in 空闲 (kòngxián, 'free time') and 闲聊 (xiánliáo, 'to chat casually').

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惨 describes a heart-wrenching, miserable feeling.
参 (cān) gives a sound very close to cǎn, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.english: This accident was very tragic.
example.fact: 惨 describes something tragic or miserable, and appears in 悲惨 (bēicǎn, 'tragic') and 惨重 (cǎnzhòng, 'heavy, disastrous').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洁 describes something washed and made clean and pure.
吉 (jí) gives a sound close to jié, sharing the initial — the rhyme has drifted slightly from í to ié.

example.hanzi: 她把房间打扫得很整洁。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo de hěn zhěngjié.
example.english: She swept the room until it was very tidy.
example.fact: 洁 almost always appears in 整洁 (zhěngjié, 'tidy') and 清洁 (qīngjié, 'clean'), rather than alone.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踪 names the footprints or tracks left behind.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踪.

example.english: The police are tracking down leads.
example.fact: 踪 almost always appears in 追踪 (zhuīzōng, 'to track') and 踪迹 (zōngjì, 'traces, tracks').

components.note: 力 (strength) — 勃 describes a sudden burst of energy or strength.
孛 gives a sound closely related to bó, sharing the initial b-.

example.english: The company's business is booming.
example.fact: 勃 almost always appears in 蓬勃 (péngbó, 'vigorous, flourishing') and 勃然 (bórán, 'suddenly, abruptly').

etymologyHint: A solider 兵 quartered under one's roof 宀

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 宾 describes someone welcomed under one's roof.
兵 (soldier) — a soldier 兵 quartered under one's roof 宀 gave 宾 its meaning 'guest, visitor.'

example.english: Welcome, all guests.
example.fact: 宾 is a formal word for 'guest,' appearing in 来宾 (láibīn, 'visiting guest') and 宾馆 (bīnguǎn, 'hotel').

example.english: He travels for work very frequently.
example.fact: 频 almost always appears in 频繁 (pínfán, 'frequent') and 频率 (pínlǜ, 'frequency').

components.note: 亻 (person) — 仇 describes a person one holds a grudge against, 'an enemy.'
九 (jiǔ) is only distantly related in sound to chóu — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.english: The two families have a feud.
example.fact: 仇 means 'enmity, a grudge,' and appears in 仇人 (chóurén, 'enemy') and 报仇 (bàochóu, 'to take revenge').

components.note: 石 (stone) — 磨 names a millstone, or the act of grinding with one.
麻 (má) shares the initial m- and tone with mó, though the rhyme has drifted slightly from á to ó.

example.english: She is sharpening a knife.
example.fact: 磨 is the everyday verb for grinding or sharpening, and appears in 磨刀 ('to sharpen a knife') and 磨练 (móliàn, 'to temper oneself through hardship').

meanings: to hand over; to pass on; to deliver
(bound form) progressively; in the proper order

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 递 describes passing something along by moving it from one person to another.
弟 (dì) gives the sound — an exact match with 递.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ yán dì gěi wǒ.
example.english: Please pass me the salt.
example.fact: 递 is the everyday verb for handing something over, and appears in 快递 (kuàidì, 'express delivery').

example.english: This idea is a bit strange.
example.fact: 邪 means 'evil, wrong,' and appears in 邪恶 (xié'è, 'evil') and the colloquial 邪门 (xiémén, 'strange, fishy').

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撞 describes striking or bumping into something with force.
童 (tóng) is only distantly related in sound to zhuàng — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, bié zhuàng dào qiáng shàng.
example.english: Be careful, don't crash into the wall.
example.fact: 撞 is the everyday verb for bumping or crashing into something, and appears in 撞车 (zhuàngchē, 'car collision').
